articles.title: Dajaune Brown Scores Twice as Rochdale Defeats Fleetwood Town 2-1
articles.excerpt: Dajaune Brown, on loan from Derby County, has found his scoring form at Rochdale, contributing to a recent victory over Fleetwood Town.
articles.content_html:
Dajaune Brown, a 20-year-old striker on loan from Derby County, has made a significant impact at Rochdale, scoring twice in recent matches. After a challenging previous season, Brown has rediscovered his form in League Two, helping Rochdale secure a 2-1 victory against Fleetwood Town last weekend.

Brown's journey began in Derby County's youth academy, where he showcased his goal-scoring abilities. He had a successful loan spell at Gateshead in the National League, netting nine goals and providing eight assists in 22 games. However, injuries hampered his progress in the following season, leading to a less productive loan at Port Vale, where he scored only three goals in 34 appearances as the team faced relegation from League One.

Since joining Rochdale in the summer, Brown initially struggled to find the net, going six games without a goal. However, he broke his drought with a goal in Rochdale's 2-0 win over Oldham Athletic, followed by his impressive performance against Fleetwood Town, where he scored one goal and assisted another. Rochdale manager Jim Watson praised Brown's contributions, stating, "Yes, beautiful goal. That’s two and two for him. So, [the goals] gives him a lot of confidence."

Rochdale's recent form, bolstered by Brown's resurgence, is crucial as they aim to improve their standing in League Two. Fans will be eager to see if Brown can maintain his scoring streak in upcoming fixtures, as the team looks to build on their recent successes.

articles.title: Heywood Man Receives Suspended Sentence for Cocaine Supply
articles.excerpt: Joshua Carroll, 36, from Heywood, has been given a suspended 30-month prison sentence for possessing cocaine with intent to supply, following a court ruling on September 29, 2026.

A 36-year-old man from Heywood has been handed a suspended 30-month prison sentence for possessing cocaine with intent to supply. Joshua Carroll, of Peel Lane, pleaded guilty to the charges at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on September 1, 2026, with the offences occurring in Rochdale on July 1, 2022.

The sentencing took place at Manchester Crown Court on September 29, 2026. The court suspended the sentence for two years, meaning Carroll will avoid custody if he adheres to the conditions set by the court. He is required to complete 150 hours of unpaid work and pay £150 in prosecution costs along with a £228 surcharge.

In addition to the suspended sentence, the court ordered the forfeiture and destruction of drugs and related items seized during the investigation. Carroll was also ordered to forfeit £21,141.71 in cash linked to the drug offences. He will be under supervision for two years as part of his sentence, and a collection order mandates that he make payments by March 29, 2027.

This case highlights ongoing efforts to combat drug-related crime in the area. Local residents may see continued police activity as authorities work to address drug supply issues in Rochdale and surrounding areas.

articles.title: Tram Services Resume on Oldham to Rochdale Line Following Track Replacement
articles.excerpt: Tram services have resumed on the Oldham to Rochdale line after essential track replacement work was completed, part of a £150m investment in Greater Manchester's tram network.
articles.content_html:
Tram services have resumed on the Oldham to Rochdale line after essential track replacement work was successfully completed. This marks a significant milestone in the summer programme of network improvements aimed at enhancing the Greater Manchester tram system.

The work involved a planned two-week closure between Victoria and Rochdale town centre and is part of a wider £150 million investment to maintain and improve the tram network. Engineers worked around the clock to replace 1.2 kilometres of track, improve drainage, renew foundations, and correct the alignment and level of the track. This complex operation utilised approximately 290 new concrete sleepers, 2,000 tonnes of gravel, and over 5,000 tonnes of ballast.

As a result of the improvements, sections of the route that previously required speed restrictions can now operate at normal speeds of up to 50 mph, which is expected to enhance journey times for passengers. Ian Davies, Network Director for Metrolink at Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM), stated that this engineering work will significantly improve the reliability and long-term condition of the network.

Further improvement work is scheduled to take place at various locations across the Bee Network in the coming months, with significant projects planned at Trafford Bar and Deansgate-Castlefield. During this time, there will be no trams on the Eccles, Trafford Centre, or Altrincham lines for three weeks from Monday, 13th July to Sunday, 2nd August.

articles.title: Renovation of College Bank's Seven Sisters Towers Could Take Over a Decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the Seven Sisters tower blocks in College Bank would displace residents for more than ten years, as discussions continue on the future of the iconic buildings.
articles.content_html:
Housing chiefs have warned that renovating the Seven Sisters tower blocks in College Bank could take more than a decade, displacing residents for the entire duration of the work. This statement comes as Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has yet to make a decision regarding the future of the iconic buildings, which have been a part of Rochdale's skyline for 61 years.

Residents have expressed their desire for refurbishment rather than demolition and have sought support from Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. The scale of the renovation required to bring the buildings up to modern standards is significant, and RBH has indicated that the blocks would not be habitable until the work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in earnest in 2017, when RBH first raised concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their life. In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping to see the towers restored through a partnership between RBH and Legal and General Affordable Homes. However, this partnership was dissolved in September 2024, leading to further uncertainty for residents.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Recent surveys conducted by RBH revealed that the blocks are not safe for continued occupation, necessitating the relocation of residents. As discussions progress, the future of the Seven Sisters remains uncertain, with the community keenly awaiting a resolution.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: A look at the rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel, the documentary history of Healey Dell and how 19th‑century storytellers turned landscape into legend.
articles.summary: A look at the rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel, the documentary history of Healey Dell and how 19th‑century storytellers turned landscape into legend.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is one of this borough’s best‑known beauty spots: a steep, wooded stretch of the River Spodden with waterfalls, industrial‑archaeology remains and a striking Victorian viaduct. The site is managed as a local nature reserve and promoted locally for wildlife, walks and family trails. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Documented history

The clearest, verifiable facts are straightforward. The most visible man‑made landmark is the Healey Dell (or Spodden Valley) viaduct, a stone railway viaduct built in 1869–70 now recorded on the National Heritage List for England (Grade II). That listing records the viaduct’s date and architectural features and is the official source for its historic status. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

Healey Dell is also recognised locally for its wildlife and industrial remains: former mill sites, reservoirs and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line that became a walking route. The patchwork of conservation designations and local management explains why the Dell has been preserved and interpreted for visitors rather than being redeveloped; local authority material and planning records identify the area as a Local Nature Reserve and a valued Site of Biological Importance. Where administrative or planning details are time‑sensitive (for example management plans or conservation grants), the public record on council and planning sites should be checked for the latest dates and decisions. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

Folklore and the Fairies’ Chapel

The “Fairies’ Chapel” is a small rock niche and cascade on the River Spodden, a feature visitors have long noticed because the hollowed rock and its small pool suggest a miniature, church‑like space. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre acknowledge that the alcove’s appearance is the result of water‑erosion acting on the bedrock, and they also present the traditional tales that grew up around the spot. Those tales are storytelling and interpretation layered on top of the physical place, not separate documentary records of events. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

The best‑known written record of the tales dates to the 19th century. John Roby, a collector of Lancashire legends, printed versions of the Healey Dell stories — including the account of an enchanted chapel, a Fairy Queen and the Healey Dwarf — in his Traditions of Lancashire. Roby’s volumes are important as records of local storytelling, but they are not documentary proof of supernatural events; Roby himself compiled and reworked oral tradition and local romance for a Victorian readership. If you want the earliest printed versions of the tale, Roby is the primary source. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

What the stories say (and what we can verify)

There are several overlapping strands in local versions: an enchanted cavern where fairies held court; a small figure sometimes called the Healey Dwarf; prophecies and encounters that befall local characters; and a dramatic episode in which witches are turned to stone. These elements are part of oral tradition and poetic retellings and are preserved in Victorian collections and modern retellings by local heritage groups. They are folklore—useful for understanding local culture and Victorian taste in storytelling—but they are not reducible to verifiable events in the historical record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

How the Dell uses the stories today

Local interpretation deliberately keeps both threads — the real, documentable history and the folkloric — visible. The heritage centre, council walking guides and family trails present the Fairies’ Chapel as a natural feature with a storytelling past: a way to engage visitors, especially children, with nature and local memory. If you are looking for archival evidence that fairies or witch‑turnings actually occurred, none exists in the way a historian would accept; what exists instead are printed and oral traditions and the physical niche that inspired them. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

If you visit

Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as you would any feature of local heritage: enjoy the setting, respect the riverside ecology, and remember that much of what makes the Dell magical is human imagination shaped by landscape. For anyone curious about the sources behind the stories, the 19th‑century collections and the council and heritage centre materials are the best starting points — Roby for the printed tradition, Historic England and the council for the site’s verifiable history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/15271/pg15271-images.html))

articles.title: Rochdale Council Wins Legal Battle Over Hopwood Hall Sale
articles.excerpt: A two-day trial in the High Court will determine the future of Hopwood Hall, as Hopwood DePree seeks to reclaim his ancestral home from Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
A trial concerning the ownership of Hopwood Hall commenced today in the High Court in Manchester, with Hopwood DePree contesting Rochdale Council's control over the historic manor house. DePree, a descendant of the Hopwood family who constructed the hall in the 1420s, argues that the council has reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the property after he invested seven years in its restoration.

The hall, which has been owned by Rochdale Council since it was acquired from private hands in the 1980s, is a Grade II-listed building. The council had previously entered into an exclusivity agreement with DePree, but in November 2024, they announced plans to explore other options, citing a lack of a 'commercially viable' business model from him.

DePree's legal action follows the council's decision to end the exclusivity agreement, which he claims was unjustified after planning permission was granted for the site in 2022. He contends that the conditions for the transfer of ownership have been met and is seeking a court ruling to enforce the agreement.

The outcome of this trial could significantly impact the future of Hopwood Hall, which has historical importance and has suffered from neglect over the years. The court's decision is expected to clarify the ownership status and potential future developments for the site.

articles.title: Seven Arrested in Police Raids Uncovering Cannabis Farms in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Seven individuals have been arrested after police uncovered three cannabis farms during coordinated raids across the Rochdale district, involving over 50 officers.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

08:26, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested after police conducted early morning raids at six addresses across the Rochdale district, uncovering three cannabis farms and seizing drugs and cash.

08:17, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested after police uncovered three cannabis farms during coordinated raids across the Rochdale district, involving over 50 officers.

07:11, 02 October 2026

A police operation across Rochdale has led to the arrest of seven individuals and the dismantling of three cannabis farms, following months of intelligence gathering.

06:39, 02 October 2026

Seven individuals have been arrested in connection with three cannabis farms discovered during police raids across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton. The operation involved over 50 officers and resulted in the seizure of drugs, cash, and a stolen vehicle.

04:43, 02 October 2026

Greater Manchester Police have arrested seven individuals and shut down multiple cannabis farms in a coordinated operation across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton.

Seven people have been arrested following a series of police raids that uncovered three cannabis farms across the Rochdale district. The operation, which involved more than 50 officers, took place early on Thursday morning and targeted six addresses in areas including Heywood, Middleton, and Newhey.

The raids were the culmination of several months of intelligence gathering by Greater Manchester Police, aimed at dismantling organised crime groups operating in the region. During the searches, police seized a significant number of cannabis plants, cash, Class A drugs, and a vehicle suspected to be stolen.

Among those arrested were a 33-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman, both suspected of cultivating cannabis and abstracting electricity. Additionally, a 61-year-old man and a 61-year-old woman were arrested on similar charges. A 35-year-old man was taken into custody on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A drugs, while a 28-year-old man was arrested for possession with intent to supply Class B drugs. A 78-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of handling stolen property.

Dr Palmer has a long-standing connection with Rochdale, having collaborated with local cultural organisations and partners, including Touchstones Rochdale and Rochdale Council. In her role as chair, Dr Palmer will provide independent leadership for Rochdale Creates, supporting partners in delivering the borough’s shared cultural vision. Her focus will be on strengthening collaboration across sectors and ensuring that culture continues to play a central role in Rochdale’s regeneration, wellbeing, community pride, and economic growth.

Rochdale Creates, established in 2022, is a partnership that unites cultural organisations, artists, educators, businesses, community groups, and public sector partners. The Compact aims to champion culture as a driver of regeneration and economic opportunity, and Dr Palmer's leadership is expected to enhance its governance and long-term sustainability.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: A small, stubbornly local verb that names the familiar ankle-twist — where it comes from, how local it really is, and what dialect research tells us.
articles.summary: A small, stubbornly local verb that names the familiar ankle-twist — where it comes from, how local it really is, and what dialect research tells us.
articles.body:
Anyone from parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” In local use, cruckle (sometimes heard and written crookle) most commonly names that sudden roll or twist of the foot you can usually walk off but will still wince about. It is a compact, expressive verb and — crucially for dialect researchers — one that locals readily name when talking about the town’s speech.

Where the word comes from

Cruckle sits in a larger family of northern English and Scots dialect words meaning to bend, crouch, stoop or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect lexicography records forms such as crookle and crookl(e) with senses like “to make crooked, to bend, to stoop.” Those older entries fit the meaning Rochdalians use today: a bending or awkward movement of the foot or body. The frequentative or diminutive suffix ‑le (present in many dialect verbs) and the root crook/krug (suggesting a hook or bend) help explain how crook → crookle → cruckle developed as a natural dialect shape.

Scots dialect dictionaries record closely related forms (cruggle, kruggle, krukel and cruckle) meaning to crouch or huddle, showing that the same verbal pattern has a wide historical reach across the north of Britain rather than being invented in Rochdale overnight.

How strongly it’s tied to Rochdale

People in and around Greater Manchester often treat cruckle as a Rochdale‑flavoured word. That perception is borne out in recent perceptual dialect research: a 2024 draw‑a‑map study of folk labels for Greater Manchester speech collected comments from local residents and recorded words people used to describe particular places’ speech. One respondent’s list of keywords describing Rochdale included “broad, flat, cruckle, guinnel,” showing that cruckle is part of the way some locals and neighbouring residents characterise Rochdale speech.

Two points follow from this. First, cruckle is not uniquely Rochdale in the sense of being unprecedented elsewhere — cognate forms appear across northern dialect sources — but second, modern speakers strongly associate the form cruckle with Rochdale in ordinary folk talk. In short: historically widespread roots, locally strong identity.

What dialect research tells us

Two kinds of evidence are useful. Historical lexicography (the English Dialect Dictionary and related sources) documents the older verb family and its meanings; linguistic geography and perceptual dialectology show how people today attach words to places. Together they give a plausible account: cruckle is a predictable local survival and reshaping of a long‑standing northern dialect verb, and contemporary perception maps show Rochdale as one of the places where the word still figures in local descriptions.

A word of caution on origins and legends

The word also crops up in occasional local place‑name commentary (for example a “Cruckles Well” recorded in historic notes for other towns) and in popular lists of regional words. Those claims can be interesting but are often speculative: where a place‑name appears to link to an old dialect word, that link is a plausible hypothesis rather than a proven etymology unless supported by dated documentary evidence. In other words, treat folktales and place‑name suggestions as tradition or interpretation, not as the same thing as documented lexical history.

Why it matters locally

Small words like cruckle matter because they carry local identity. They are ways people name shared experience (that sudden ankle‑twist) and, in doing so, mark membership of a place. Dialect scholars treat such words as data: they help map the geography of speech, the memory of older forms, and how communities talk about their own language. For Rochdale, cruckle is a neat example of a living piece of the borough’s verbal landscape — historically rooted, regionally connected, and distinctly local in everyday perception.

If you want to follow up

Authoritative historical lexica (the English Dialect Dictionary and Scots dialect dictionaries) show the older family of forms; recent perceptual research in the Journal of Linguistic Geography (2024) documents cruckle as one of the folk‑terms people associate with Rochdale. If a fuller historical proof for any single place‑name link is required, that should be sought in dated local records or place‑name studies rather than in modern recollection.

Bottom line: cruckle is not a made‑up novelty — it’s a local survival of an old northern verb pattern — and while related forms exist elsewhere, local speakers and recent research both show that the word is especially, and recognisably, Rochdalian today.

articles.title: Supermarkets Urged to Address Litter Issues Along Rochdale Canal
articles.excerpt: A litter picking group has called on Aldi, Morrisons, and Tesco to take action after repeatedly retrieving trolleys from the Rochdale canal, highlighting ongoing litter problems in the area.
articles.content_html:
A litter picking group in Failsworth has urged Aldi, Morrisons, and Tesco to take action regarding the increasing number of supermarket trolleys found in the Rochdale canal. The group, Clean Up Failsworth Canal, has been active for over 13 years, conducting monthly clean-ups along the canal, where they regularly encounter discarded trolleys, flytipped rubbish, and other litter.

On September 20, the group collected 22 bags of rubbish, 26 nitrous oxide canisters, and 17 supermarket trolleys from the canal. Sandra Ball, a local councillor representing Failsworth West for Reform UK, expressed frustration over the ongoing issue, stating that the supermarkets need to 'get their act together' to prevent trolleys from being dumped in the water. She noted that the problem has persisted for years, with some clean-up sessions yielding as many as 20 trolleys.

The litter picking efforts are supported by Oldham Council and the Canal and River Trust, with around 90 volunteers participating in the initiative. Despite their hard work, Ball described the situation as 'disheartening', as litter reappears almost immediately after clean-ups. Local resident Lesley Halliday, who participates in the clean-ups with her grandson, echoed these sentiments, highlighting the frustration of seeing litter reappear shortly after it has been removed.

In response to the concerns, a spokesperson for Morrisons stated that they make efforts to retrieve abandoned trolleys as soon as they are made aware of them. Tesco also encouraged customers to return their trolleys and mentioned that they employ a specialist company to handle abandoned trolleys. The ongoing litter issues in the canal raise concerns about the local environment and the impact on community efforts to maintain a clean and pleasant area.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Wins High Court Case Against Hopwood DePree
articles.excerpt: An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton for £1 after a High Court ruling.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

02:08, 01 October 2026

An American man has lost his legal bid to take ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton for £1 after a High Court ruling.

Rochdale Council has successfully defended its ownership of Hopwood Hall in Middleton after a High Court judge ruled against Hopwood DePree, who sought to acquire the Grade II-listed mansion for £1. DePree, an American actor and filmmaker, claimed ancestral ties to the property and argued that a 2017 agreement with the council entitled him to purchase the hall following the securing of planning permission for its restoration and redevelopment.

Judge David Hodge KC found that the conditions necessary for the transfer of ownership had not been met. Despite its current dilapidated state, the court noted that Hopwood Hall is among the top 10% of most important listed buildings in England. DePree's plans included transforming the hall into a wedding venue, hotel, and visitor attractions to revive the historic site.

In 2022, Rochdale Council decided against transferring ownership to DePree and subsequently barred him and a group of volunteers from accessing the site. DePree expressed his disappointment following the ruling, stating that he had hoped to restore the hall to its former glory.

The council's victory in this case reinforces its commitment to preserving the historic significance of Hopwood Hall, which remains a key landmark in the area. The ruling also means that the council will retain control over any future developments concerning the property.
